nodes.title: Overview

fields.label: Method type
fields.value: Multi-site direct replication of 13 effects, bundled into one standardized online-administered session; cross-site moderation analysis

fields.label: Summary
fields.value: Replicability of 13 effects tested across 36 independent samples totaling 6,344 participants; aggregate and site-level moderation by lab versus online and US versus international.

nodes.summary: Many Labs replication of 13 effects across 36 samples

fields.label: Question
fields.value: Variation in replicability of 13 classic and contemporary psychological effects across 36 samples and settings

fields.label: Gap
fields.value: Little attempt has been made to assess the variation in replicability of findings across samples and research contexts.

fields.label: Contribution
fields.value: Establish a paradigm for testing replicability across samples and settings and provide a rich data set

fields.label: Setting
fields.value: 36 samples: 27 data collections in a laboratory and 9 conducted online; 25 from the US, 11 from other countries

fields.label: Recruitment
fields.value: Site leads were recruited through the Open Science Collaboration forum and the SPSP Discussion List; each site recruited its own participants and coordinated its own data collection.

fields.label: Eligibility
fields.value: Site-level inclusion: follow local ethical procedures, administer the protocol as specified, collect data from at least 80 participants, post a video simulation of the setting, and document recruiting, sample and protocol changes. Participant-level eligibility is limited in Table 1 to US-only for MTurk and Project Implicit samples.

fields.label: N (all samples)
fields.value: 6,344 participants across 36 samples (one sample had N = 79)

fields.label: Roles
fields.value: All participants are AI participants in the replay; laboratory experimenters did not interact with participants unless asked and were unaware of condition, so no scripted role is needed.

fields.label: Participant characteristics per site
fields.value: Age, race and ethnicity, political ideology, country of citizenship, native language, major and prior exposure were collected; per-site values are in Table S1, which is not in the provided supplement.

fields.label: Compensation
fields.value: Not reported per site in the paper or provided supplement (Appendix B only lists the question that was asked of site leads)

fields.label: Design type
fields.value: Twelve short studies bundled in one session; with the exception of one correlational study, each is a simple two-condition design

fields.label: Order
fields.value: Studies presented in randomized order, except the math IAT and its explicit measures always last

fields.label: Blinding
fields.value: Laboratory experimenters were not aware of participant condition for each task

fields.label: Manipulation check
fields.value: An instructional manipulation check (IMC) after the studies; it was not analyzed further for this report

fields.label: Task
fields.value: A paragraph of introduction, then the studies in randomized order (math IAT and explicit measures always last), then an instructional manipulation check, a short demographic questionnaire, and the moderator measures for flag priming; debrief at the end

fields.label: Medium
fields.value: All replications were conducted via computer on the Project Implicit infrastructure; materials translated into the dominant language of each country

fields.label: Where exact wording is
fields.value: Exact wording for each study, including a link to the study, is in the supplementary materials; the supplement provided links to the OSF page.

All told, the main conclusion from this small sample of studies is that, to predict effect size, it is much more important to know what effect is being studied than to know the sample or setting in which it is being studied.

At the same time, this conclusion is surely constrained by the small, nonrandom sample of studies represented here. issues.title: The IAT records response latencies, which a text-only AI participant cannot produce
issues.reason: The IAT is scored from trial-by-trial reaction times (D algorithm); a text model answering in prose has no latencies.
issues.impact: Effects 12 and 13 cannot be replayed as published with text participants; any simulation would need a different instrument and must be labelled an adaptation.
issues.suggestedAction: Decide whether to exclude this study from AI runs or design a labelled adaptation.

issues.title: The paper's text disagrees on how many effects replicated
issues.reason: The abstract and results say 10 of 13 effects replicated (imagined contact weak, two not replicated); the Discussion says eleven of 13 were successfully replicated.
issues.impact: A replay summary could quote either count; the program records both as reported.
issues.suggestedAction: Treat 10 of 13 (results and abstract) as the main count unless the researcher decides otherwise.

issues.title: Rank-transformed anchoring statistics in the supplement look internally inconsistent
issues.reason: The supplement lists Anchoring 1 (NYC) with t(5607)=90.49, d=1.17 and Anchoring 4 (babies) with the same t(5607)=90.49, while Table 2 gives NYC t=42.86 and babies t=90.49.
issues.impact: Anchoring comparison values may be mis-transcribed in the supplement.
issues.suggestedAction: Use the Table 2 values as primary and check against the OSF data.

issues.title: SF–NY anchoring: unit label differs between the instrument document and the study page
issues.reason: Measures_US_Version labels the answer box for the 'shorter than 6,000 miles' item “(babies)”, but the study page anchoring1b.html labels it “(miles)”. Materials use “(miles)”, as in the study page and the low-anchor version.
issues.impact: A wrong unit label could change how participants answer that item.
issues.suggestedAction: Confirm “(miles)” is correct, or supply the label as run.

issues.title: Flag priming: the manipulation is a set of photographs
issues.reason: The four photos differ between flag and control conditions; the instrument document only has screenshot placeholders and the paper says only that the flag appears in two of four photos. A text-only AI participant cannot see them, and the sources hold no verbatim description.
issues.impact: Without the photos both arms would read identically, so the study is excluded from text runs.
issues.suggestedAction: Decide whether to run it with a vision-capable model and the images in sources/materials_html/images, or leave it out.
